name: Török Bank House (Szervita Square)
intro: Török Bank House at Szervita tér 3, in the Inner City of Pest, is a four-storey Secession commercial building that the heritage register attributes to Henrik Böhm and Ármin Hegedűs and dates to 1906. It is best known for the large glazed upper floor and the Miksa Róth mosaic in its gable, both easy to admire from the square below.
about: The Török Bank House, in Hungarian the Török Bankház, is the former headquarters of a lottery and banking firm. The national heritage register lists it as a Secession commercial building by Henrik Böhm and Ármin Hegedűs, dated 1906. It has four storeys on a U-shaped plan and a façade of three axes, and it was built as offices and housing in a closed row of buildings on Szervita tér in the fifth district.

The sight is the façade, and it rewards a slow look upwards. On the top floor a large glass surface with three semicircular-arched windows is separated from the lower floors by cornices. Above it rises a monumental gable framed in curved and broken-arch stonework, with two winged head sculptures beneath a broken-arched opening. In the gable sits a coloured mosaic by Miksa Róth, which the register titles Hungária megdicsőülése, the Glorification of Hungaria. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that the Virgin Mary as Patrona Hungariae stands at its centre and describes it as the largest mosaic composition in Budapest.

The building is in private use and is not open as a museum, so the experience is an exterior one: you look at it from the pavement and the square rather than going inside. The register lists it as an office and residential building, and the ground floor carries shop portals.

The house stands in the Inner City, in the dense commercial centre of Pest and a good place to look at Secession-era street fronts. It makes an easy pause on a walk between Váci Street, Vörösmarty Square and the Danube embankment, and its upper storeys are best seen in daylight, when the mosaic's colours and the glazed floor show clearly.
tips: Treat it as a façade stop: stand back in the square and look up, because the glass floor, gable and mosaic are all on the upper levels and the ground floor carries shop portals.
Bring a lens or phone zoom that can pick out the mosaic and the winged head sculptures in the gable, and photograph in daylight when the colours are clearest.
The building is in private use, so keep voices down and do not enter stairwells or courtyards unless a business there invites you in.
Pair it with Váci Street and Vörösmarty Square nearby, or with the guide to downtown Pest on foot.

history.intro: The building was made for a firm that lived off the Hungarian class lottery, and its design came from a competition that the winners did not get to build.

sections.heading: A lottery firm becomes a joint-stock bank
paragraphs: According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the Török firm was founded in 1897, the year Hungary replaced its lottery with a class lottery whose tickets and prizes were handled by private financial houses. On 8 May 1906 the business became a joint-stock company under the name Török A. és Társa Bankház Részvénytársaság. Its slogan, Török szerencséje örök, became a popular catchphrase. The article notes that Török A. may not have been a real person. Of the executives whose names survive, it gives information only about Mátyás Stein, who came from Hamburg around 1895, and it presumes that he was the firm's leading official from the start.

sections.heading: The plot and the competition, 1905–1906
paragraphs: Before the move to Szervita tér the bank had premises on Váci körút and then Teréz körút. In 1905 Mátyás Stein bought the Szervita tér plot, where a two-storey house stood; the house was demolished but its strong cellar was kept. A design competition was won by Géza Aladár Kármán and Gyula Ullmann, yet the building was constructed to the design of the runners-up, Henrik Böhm and Ármin Hegedűs. The heritage register gives 1906 as the date of the building.

sections.heading: After the bank
paragraphs: Above the mosaic an illuminated glass globe once stood, held by Atlas and a biblical couple; the group was removed in 1939. The bank's business ended after the Second World War. The ground floor then became a shop and entrance, the upper offices were converted into flats, and an instrumentation institute of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences also moved in, as Hungarian Wikipedia describes. The building is a protected monument, listed in the register under number 621; a 2014 note there rates its condition as good.

name: Hármashatár-hegy and the Guckler Károly Lookout
address: Hármashatár-hegy summit, boundary of Budapest II and III districts
intro: Hármashatár-hegy is a 495-metre summit in the northern Buda Hills, on the boundary of Budapest's second and third districts. Its Guckler Károly Lookout, opened in 2016, gives a full panorama over the city and the Danube, and the National Blue Trail reaches the hill from Hűvösvölgy and from the outer Bécsi út.
about: Hármashatár-hegy is the central summit of a rock group in the north-north-eastern part of the Buda Hills. It rises 495 metres above sea level on the boundary of Budapest's II and III districts and also belongs to Solymár. The hill is mostly dolomite, and its eastern slope drops steeply towards the Danube: Hungarian Wikipedia gives a height difference of over 400 metres within about two kilometres, the largest in the range.

The main sight is the Guckler Károly Lookout, which stands on the summit and gives a full 360-degree view of Budapest, the Danube and the surrounding hills. A tourism listing says that on clear days the view reaches the Mátra. The same listing adds that the National Blue Trail reaches the lookout from Hűvösvölgy and from the outer Bécsi út.

Around the summit lies a small recreation complex. The Rotter Lajos tourist house, named after a glider pilot, was opened in 2016 in a rebuilt former pilots' lodge, and the old hangars now hold a forest school, a bistro and an event venue. A playground themed on flight and local wildlife was added beside it in December 2021.

The place suits a half-day on foot rather than a quick stop. It sits among forest paths, and works well as a walk with a reward at the top for anyone who enjoys the Buda Hills and a wide view over the city.
tips: The National Blue Trail reaches the lookout from Hűvösvölgy (near the Children's Railway terminus) and from the outer Bécsi út; allow time and wear proper walking footwear.
Visibility decides the view, so check the weather before you set out.
Check the current status of the lookout, the tourist house and the other facilities with the forest company or the district's official channels before you go, as conditions on the hill can change.
Stay on the marked paths, take your rubbish home and keep dogs under control, since the hill is a working forest and a nature area.
Combine the hike with the Hűvösvölgy end of the Children's Railway.

history.intro: The hill has a long record under several names, and the present lookout is the result of a forest-company redevelopment of the 2010s.

sections.heading: A boundary hill with a long record
paragraphs: A boundary survey of 1212 refers to the hill as Mons Excelsus, the High Mountain. In 1847, during the naming of land plots, it was called Árpád orma, a name that did not catch on. The present name came in the 19th century, and until 1873 the summit marked the point where the lands of Buda, Óbuda and Pesthidegkút met.

sections.heading: Guckler, the path and the early tourist house
paragraphs: The lookout is named after Károly Guckler, a forester who led reforestation on the hill. In 1917–1918 he had a walking path of 3.5 kilometres built on its eastern side. A tourist house opened on the summit in 1926, a road to the top followed in 1928, and in April 1940 the Petőfi Sándor Flight School opened there.

sections.heading: Redevelopment and the 2016 lookout
paragraphs: In 1994 the state contributed the 146-hectare summit property to the Pilisi Parkerdő forestry company; Hungarian Wikipedia reports that the ownership registration has since been disputed in court. The Óbuda municipality reports that from 2012 the company began revitalising the hill as an eco-tourism centre that also honours its aviation past. A forest school opened in spring 2014, and construction of the lookout and tourist house began in 2015. The tourist house was designed by the Ybl Prize-winning architect Koller József.

According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the lookout was opened to hikers on 8 April 2016 and officially inaugurated on 14 July 2016. In November 2018 the forestry company installed information boards, two viewing terraces and rest areas along the path and renamed it the Guckler Károly Nature Trail.

name: Tabán Church of St Catherine of Alexandria
intro: The Tabán Church of St Catherine of Alexandria is the Roman Catholic parish church of the Tabán, on Attila út below Castle Hill. A Baroque church that grew from an Ottoman mosque converted into a chapel in 1686, it survived the 20th-century clearance of a district that was otherwise largely demolished.
about: The Tabán church is a Roman Catholic parish church at Attila út 11 in Budapest's first district, dedicated to Saint Catherine of Alexandria. It is a Baroque building, and it stands on the site of a mosque of Sokollu Mustafa, Pasha of Buda. That origin is the thing to know about the church: the Catholic chapel made from the mosque in 1686 became the nucleus of the building seen today.

The façade goes back to a remodelling of 1880–81 in an eclectic style, simplified in the post-war reconstruction, and the statues of Saint Catherine, Saint Gellért and Saint Charles Borromeo are by Szász Gyula (1881). Inside, the parish's own description lists a high-altar painting by Marastoni Jakab dated 1850 and a pulpit of 1822; its list of organs runs from Hartman (1798) and Focht Károly (1834–35) to a Rieger Otto organ of 1905. In the vestibule hangs a copy of the Tabáni Krisztus, a Romanesque relief fragment from the 12th century whose original belongs to the Budapest History Museum.

The church sits on a hillside beneath Castle Hill and Gellért Hill, next to the approach to the Elisabeth Bridge. Much of the old Tabán around it was swept away in the 20th century and part of the area became a park, so the church today stands as a rare historic building in a green setting rather than inside a dense old quarter.

It is a living parish, not a museum: the parish website lists regular Masses, sacramental preparation and community events. The physician Semmelweis Ignác was baptised here, as the parish history records. Visitors should treat it as a place of worship and check the parish website for current visiting arrangements.
tips: This is an active church, so dress modestly, speak quietly and avoid walking around during Mass or other services; ask before photographing inside.
Check the parish website for the current times when the church can be visited, and for any services or events that may affect a visit.
Look for the statues on the façade and, in the vestibule, the copy of the Tabán Christ relief; the original is in the Budapest History Museum on Castle Hill.
The Tabán park, Gellért Hill and the Rudas thermal bath are all nearby, which makes the church an easy stop on a walk between the river and the hills.

history.intro: The church's history runs from an Ottoman mosque through Baroque rebuilding to fire, war and a major reconstruction, as the parish's own history page sets out.

sections.heading: From mosque to parish church, 1686–1702
paragraphs: A mosque of Sokollu Mustafa, Pasha of Buda, stood on the site; the sources differ on the date, since the parish gives 1566–1578 as the years of his term as pasha, while Hungarian Wikipedia says he built the mosque in 1566. When the Ottomans were driven out in 1686 most of the district was destroyed, but the mosque survived, and Catholic believers converted it into a chapel that same year. The Franciscans built a school beside it in 1697, and in 1702 a parish was founded and a cemetery laid out around the chapel. Tradition holds that an older, medieval church of the area was linked to the grave of the martyr bishop Gellért, but its exact site is not known.

sections.heading: Baroque rebuilding, 1728–1777
paragraphs: Major building work began in 1728 under the master mason Obergruber Keresztély, who added a nave to the formerly square sanctuary, and most of it was complete by 1736. A crypt was built in 1749, and the foundation stone of the tower was laid on 11 August 1750 under the direction of Nöpauer Mátyás. In 1765 the deteriorating sanctuary that had come from the mosque was demolished and replaced by a new nave section and sanctuary. The churchyard cemetery was closed in 1777.

sections.heading: Fire, siege and reconstruction
paragraphs: The Great Tabán Fire of 5 September 1810 destroyed the roof structure, the tower spire and most of the furnishings, and a simple pyramidal roof replaced the spire. In 1849, during the siege of Buda, the high altar and the sanctuary fresco were destroyed. The Franciscans handed the church over to secular priests in 1868, and a major restoration in 1880–81 remodelled the façade.

The Tabán itself was reshaped in the 20th century: in 1933 much of the old district was demolished, and the Second World War destroyed most of what remained. The church was severely damaged in the war and its reconstruction lasted until the late 1960s.

name: Budapest Pinball Museum
intro: The Budapest Pinball Museum, or Flippermúzeum, is a basement full of playable pinball machines and arcade games in Újlipótváros. All machines are set to free play, so there are no coins or tokens, and play is included in the ticket. It began in 2014 as a private collection shown to the public.
about: The Flippermúzeum at Radnóti Miklós utca 18 in the thirteenth district is a hands-on museum: the exhibits are there to be played. The official site calls it Europe's leading interactive pinball museum, and states that every machine is on free play, so visitors need no coins or tokens and can play any available machine for as long as they like with a ticket.

The collection ranges widely. According to the museum it starts with the first pinball machines with flippers, from 1947, and includes video-game cabinets and other arcade games; it also reaches back to predecessors of pinball from the nineteenth century. The idea of time machines runs through the display, a phrase borrowed from a Data East pinball of that name, and the museum says it wants visitors to relive the lights, colours and sounds of an arcade childhood.

The setting is a basement in Újlipótváros; visitor guides describe underground rooms stripped back to the brick and lit by flashing lights. Visitors range from families and couples to adults who want a taste of nostalgia, and the venue can also be rented for parties and other events.

Újlipótváros is a residential district of Pest and the museum is part of its everyday life as well as a destination for visitors. Opening days differ, so it is worth checking the official contact page before you plan the trip.
tips: Check the contact page of the official website for the current days and times, and for ticket types, before you travel; they differ by weekday and can change.
The ticket includes play on every machine and artwork, so there is no need to carry coins; plan enough time to try different eras of machine.
The museum is a short walk from Margaret Bridge, so it combines with a walk in Újlipótváros or on the island.
The museum is in a basement; if step-free access matters to you, ask the museum directly, as the official page does not describe it.

history.intro: The museum began as the personal collection of a single enthusiast and grew into a venue that Hungarian and international media regularly feature.

sections.heading: From a private collection to a public museum
paragraphs: Press coverage from April 2014 reports that a pinball museum had opened in Budapest on 10 April of that year, under the name Pbal Gallery. The owner, Balázs Pálfi, had started collecting about five years earlier, beginning with a purchase on an online marketplace. The early report put the collection at 130 machines and singled out as the oldest an 1871 forerunner of pinball that resembles a wooden board.

sections.heading: Arcades, events and recognition
paragraphs: A 2026 anniversary feature, written as the museum turned twelve, lists several milestones. The Arcadia exhibition, held from 2016 to 2019, grew into what the feature calls the largest arcade-gaming event in Central Europe. In 2020 a segment of the MTV European Music Awards was broadcast from the venue, and the museum has published a Hungarian- and German-language book on Hungarian arcade history, A Flipper Múzeuma. The same feature mentions a second event venue, Game Galaxy, in Ráday utca.

The museum itself says it has been covered by international outlets including the BBC, CNN and the New York Times, and that it regularly ranks among the top attractions of Budapest on a major review site.

name: Erkel Theatre
address: II. János Pál pápa tér 30, 1087 Budapest
intro: The Erkel Theatre is a large theatre building on II. János Pál pápa tér in Józsefváros, opened in December 1911 as the Népopera, or People's Opera. With 1,819 seats it is described as Budapest's largest theatre, and since 2025 it has housed an independent musical theatre rather than a second stage of the State Opera.
about: The Erkel Theatre, in Hungarian the Erkel Színház, stands on II. János Pál pápa tér in the eighth district. It was built as the Népopera, the People's Opera, to bring opera to a wide audience, and it was designed by Jakab Dezső, Komor Marcell and Márkus Géza. English Wikipedia gives its present capacity as 1,819 seats and describes it as the largest theatre in Budapest.

Today the building is used for musical theatre. The official website lists a repertoire of musicals, with titles including A trón, Elisabeth, Rebecca and Wicked, and sells tickets for them; the titles are given in Hungarian, so check the site for the language of each production. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, at the opening in 1911 the plain auditorium was decorated only with a large fresco by Pór Bertalan; the interior was rebuilt in 1917.

The house reflects the layers of its history in its names. It began as the Népopera, later became the Városi Színház, the City Theatre, and from 1953 took the name of the composer Erkel Ferenc. For many decades it served the Hungarian State Opera as a second stage, and since 1 January 2025 it has been an independent musical theatre in the same building.

The Erkel stands in Józsefváros, on a square once called Tisza Kálmán tér. It is a performance venue, so the way to experience it is to see a show; the official website is the place to check programmes, dates and tickets.
tips: Check the official website for the current programme, performance dates and ticketing; performances are in Hungarian unless the site states otherwise.
Do not confuse it with the Hungarian State Opera House on Andrássy Avenue, which is a different building.
The plain exterior reflects the original plan: We Love Budapest reports that towers and friezes were dropped because of the cost.
The Hungarian National Museum and the Hungarian Natural History Museum are nearby in Józsefváros, so a visit to the theatre can sit alongside a museum day.

history.intro: The theatre was planned as a cheap, large opera house for the public and has changed owner, name and purpose several times since.

sections.heading: The People's Opera, 1911–1917
paragraphs: The Népopera was commissioned by a company set up for the purpose, and Jakab Dezső, Komor Marcell and Márkus Géza designed it. The capital gave the plot free for fifty years and expected Hungarian-language performances and a permanent Hungarian company in return. It was completed in nine months and opened in December 1911 on what was then Tisza Kálmán tér, with space for 3,167 people. Márkus Dezső was its first director. The enterprise lost money: according to Hungarian Wikipedia the Népopera company ceased to exist on 15 May 1915, and about half a year later the capital exercised its right and took over the theatre.

sections.heading: City Theatre and Erkel Theatre, 1917–2007
paragraphs: In 1917 the interior and stage were rebuilt to the plans of Vágó László, and capacity fell to 2,400. As the Városi Színház it was run by a series of tenants, mainly staging operettas. In 1940 it passed to a cultural-education role, from 1946 to 1948 it served as a cinema, and in 1951 it came under the State Opera. It took the name Erkel Színház in 1953. A farewell concert on 7 June 2007 preceded a closure for renovation.

sections.heading: Renovation and a new theatre, 2013 to the present
paragraphs: After a renovation led by the architect Zoboki Gábor, the theatre reopened in 2013 as a second home of the State Opera. On 28 November 2024 the government decided to set up a state-owned non-profit company to run a musical theatre in the building, and from 1 January 2025 it has operated as an independent theatre, separate from the State Opera, with Szente Vajk as managing director and Cseke Péter as artistic director. Its stated aim is to become the country's leading home for musicals.
